replacement: Socrates finished speaking, and the company applauded. Aristophanes was about to answer the allusion Socrates had made to his own speech, when suddenly there was a loud knocking at the front door, like a band of revelers, and they heard the sound of a flute-girl. Agathon told the attendants to go and see who the intruders were. 'If they are friends of ours,' he said, 'invite them in. If not, say that the drinking is over.' A little while later they heard the voice of Alcibiades booming in the courtyard. He was very drunk, and he kept roaring and shouting, 'Where is Agathon? Take me to Agathon!' At last, held up by the flute-girl and some of his attendants, he made his way to them. 'Greetings, friends,' he said, standing in the doorway with a thick garland of ivy and violets on his head and ribbons streaming down from it. 'Will you take a very drunken man as a companion in your drinking? Or shall I crown Agathon, which is why I came, and go away? I could not come yesterday, so I am here today, with these ribbons on my head. I want to take them from my own head and crown the head of this most beautiful and most wise of men, if I may call him that. Will you laugh at me because I am drunk? Yet I know very well that I am speaking the truth, even if you laugh. But first tell me: if I come in, will we have the understanding I spoke of (supra Will you have a very drunken man? etc.)?

replacement: That is good, Eryximachus, said Alcibiades; and yet it is hardly fair to compare a drunken man's speech with those of sober men. And I should like to know, my dear friend, whether you really believe what Socrates was just saying. I can assure you that the very opposite is true, and that if I praise anyone but him in his presence, whether God or man, he will hardly keep his hands off me.

replacement: So he lay down on the couch next to me, the same one on which he had eaten, and no one but the two of us was sleeping in the room. All this can be told without shame to anyone. But what follows I could hardly tell you if I were sober. Yet as the proverb says, 'In vino veritas,' whether with boys or without them (In allusion to two proverbs.); and so I must speak. Nor would I be justified in hiding the lofty actions of Socrates when I come to praise him. Besides, I have felt the serpent's sting; and he who has suffered, as they say, is willing to tell his fellow sufferers only, since they alone are likely to understand him, and will not judge harshly the words or deeds that his agony has wrung from him. For I have been bitten by something worse than a viper's tooth. I have known in my soul, or in my heart, or in some other part, the worst of pangs, more violent in a generous youth than any serpent's tooth: the pang of philosophy, which will make a man say or do anything. And you whom I see around me, Phaedrus and Agathon and Eryximachus and Pausanias and Aristodemus and Aristophanes, all of you, and I need not mention Socrates himself, have experienced the same madness and passion in your longing for wisdom. So listen, and forgive what I did then and what I say now. But let the attendants and any other uninitiated and ill-mannered persons close the doors of their ears.
